Article Title: A California homeowner was checking the crawl space beneath his house and discovered the remains of a 29-year-old woman killed in 2006; years later, police arrested her ex-husband
Article Text:
Jill Maiorca / A residential street in Big Bear Lake, California, near the Forest Road property where human remains were discovered in 2020 (SFGATE)

California homeowner discovered human remains beneath Big Bear home

Cold case team revisits unidentified remains

Jill Maiorca had been missing since 2007

Former husband arrested nearly 20 years later

Court hearing moved to October 12

A California homeowner checking the crawl space beneath his house made a disturbing discovery in October 2020 when authorities found unidentified human remains hidden beneath the property in Big Bear Lake. An autopsy determined that the person had died in a homicide, but investigators initially could not establish the victim’s identity despite DNA testing and other investigative efforts. The case remained unsolved for years until the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Cold Case Homicide Team took it up in 2023 and submitted the remains for additional DNA analysis. The testing ultimately identified the victim as Jill Maiorca, a 29-year-old woman who had been reported missing from Big Bear Lake in 2007. Investigators later identified her former husband, Jeff Maiorca, as a suspect and arrested him in September 2026.The investigation began on October 28, 2020, when deputies from the Big Bear Sheriff’s Station responded to a call about a suspicious discovery in the crawl space of a residence in the 39000 block of Forest Road in Big Bear Lake. Deputies and personnel from the Big Bear Fire Department found human remains beneath the residence and recovered them from the crawl space.An autopsy determined that the manner of death was homicide. However, investigators were initially unable to determine who the victim was. DNA testing and other investigative efforts failed to establish the person’s identity, leaving detectives with an unidentified homicide victim and no clear connection to a missing-person case. Authorities later determined that the remains had been concealed beneath the residence without the homeowner’s knowledge. Investigators have not publicly explained how or when the remains were placed there.The case received a new investigative push in 2023, when the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Cold Case Homicide Team assumed the investigation. Detectives submitted the remains for additional investigative DNA analysis in an effort to establish the victim’s identity. The additional analysis eventually produced a breakthrough. Investigators identified the remains as those of Jill Maiorca, who had been reported missing from Big Bear Lake in 2007. She was 29 years old. According to the Sheriff’s Department, evidence developed during the renewed investigation indicated that Maiorca was murdered in November 2006, approximately a year before she was reported missing. Her remains had remained unidentified for years after being discovered beneath the Forest Road residence.Maiorca’s disappearance had been recorded as a missing-person case in Big Bear Lake in 2007. Her eventual identification gave investigators a name to work with and allowed them to examine her history, relationships and circumstances surrounding her disappearance. Los Angeles County court records show that Jeff Maiorca had filed for divorce from Jill in 2004. The divorce case involved minor children, according to records cited by SFGATE. Authorities have not publicly disclosed a possible motive for Jill’s killing. They also have not detailed all the evidence that led investigators to focus on her former husband. The Sheriff’s Department has said the investigation remains ongoing.After the renewed investigation and identification of Jill’s remains, detectives identified her former husband, Jeff Maiorca, as a suspect in her murder. Maiorca, now 53, was arrested on September 21, 2026, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department. Maiorca was taken into custody without incident on September 21 and booked into Big Bear Jail on suspicion of murder, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department. The Los Angeles Times, citing incarceration records, reported that he was being held in a San Bernardino County jail without bail. SFGATE reported that Maiorca was detained at the Big Bear Lake branch library on Garstin Drive and that his arrest record listed a murder charge. Maiorca has been accused of killing Jill, but the allegations have not been adjudicated in court. Authorities have not said publicly what evidence specifically connected him to the killing or how they believe her remains came to be concealed beneath the home.According to ABC7 Los Angeles, Maiorca was initially scheduled for an arraignment on September 23, but the hearing was continued to October 12. The outlet reported that he is facing first- and second-degree murder charges, along with an enhancement alleging the use of a deadly weapon.The case remains an active homicide investigation. The Sheriff’s Department has asked anyone with information about Jill Maiorca’s disappearance or death to contact its Homicide Detail. Investigators have also said they are continuing to work on the case nearly two decades after her suspected killing.
Article Summary: California homeowner discovered human remains beneath Big Bear home in October 2020. Autopsy determined that the person had died in a homicide, but investigators initially could not establish the victim’s identity. The case remained unsolved for years until the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Cold Case Homicide Team took it up in 2023 and submitted the remains for additional DNA analysis. The testing ultimately identified the victim as Jill Maiorca, a 29-year-old woman who had been reported missing from Big Bear Lake in 2007. Investigators later identified her former husband, Jeff Maiorcan, as a suspect and arrested him in September

Article Title: Vancouver workers opened a shipping container of T-shirts and found 14 duffle bags holding 329kg of cocaine worth C$5.8 million; police say it is the city's largest-ever cocaine seizure
Article Text: Vancouver workers expecting to find boxes of T-shirts inside a shipping container instead discovered 14 duffle bags containing 328.55 kg of cocaine worth an estimated C$5.8 million, according to police. The seizure is the largest cocaine seizure in the history of the Vancouver Police Department.The drugs were discovered by employees at a legitimate Vancouver-based company while they were sorting through a shipment of T-shirts. Police said the company had ordered the clothing and had no connection to the cocaine found inside the shipment.The employees discovered the drugs and immediately contacted police. Officers were called to the business on July 21, where they seized the cocaine concealed in 14 duffle bags.“Obviously, the business was shocked by what it found. They called police right away and are in no way associated with the seized cocaine,” Sgt. Travis Fraser said in a statement.Police said the quantity of cocaine, along with stamps and packaging found with the drugs, suggests that the shipment was connected to organised crime. “This amount of drugs, as well as the stamps and packaging, clearly indicates organised crime is behind the shipment,” Fraser said.Investigators are now tracing the journey of the shipping container, which travelled through multiple countries before reaching Canada.According to police, the container left Honduras on May 18. It was then loaded onto a vessel and stopped in Jamaica on June 6. The shipment later arrived in Montreal on July 5 before eventually making its way to Vancouver.Police believe the cocaine was not supposed to reach the Vancouver company. Instead, investigators suspect the drugs were meant to be removed from the container somewhere along its journey before the shipment reached its final destination.“We believe the cocaine was supposed to be removed prior to its arrival at the company,” Fraser said. “For some reason, it was not unloaded.”The discovery has now triggered an international investigation involving authorities in several countries. Vancouver police said they are working with law enforcement agencies in Canada, Honduras, Jamaica and the United States as they try to determine who arranged the shipment and who was supposed to receive the cocaine. The investigation is also examining how the drugs were concealed among the legitimate T-shirt order and how they remained inside the container until it reached the Vancouver business.No arrests had been made at the time of the police announcement. Authorities have asked anyone with information about the shipment, the cocaine or the people involved to contact police.The seizure stands out not only because of the quantity of cocaine involved but also because of how it was discovered. Rather than being intercepted during a targeted operation, the drugs were found by employees who were simply unpacking a commercial shipment.For the Vancouver company, what appeared to be an ordinary T-shirt delivery unexpectedly became the centre of a major international drug investigation. Police are continuing to follow the shipment's route from Honduras through Jamaica and Canada as they work to identify those responsible.
Article Summary: Workers at a legitimate Vancouver-based company were sorting through a shipment of T-shirts. They found 14 duffle bags containing 328.55 kg of cocaine worth an estimated C$5.8 million. Police said the company had ordered the clothing and had no connection to the cocaine found inside the shipment.

Article Title: Priscilla Chan gave $1.48 million to a Hawaii hospital through Chan Zuckerberg Initiative; it will fund an MRI and 3D mammography machine
Article Text:
Priscilla Chan's donation will support MRI services during renovation

New 3D mammography machine will be installed

Couple have donated more than $4 million to Wilcox

Wilcox serves patients across Kauaʻi

Chan and Zuckerberg's wider Hawaii philanthropy

Dr. Priscilla Chan and her husband, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, have donated $1.48 million to Wilcox Medical Center in Līhuʻe, Hawaii, to expand advanced imaging services for patients on Kauaʻi. The donation will fund a mobile MRI unit and a new 3D mammography machine, as well as renovations needed to install the mammography equipment. The mobile MRI will allow the hospital to continue providing scans while its existing MRI suite undergoes an expected eight-month renovation. Wilcox performs more than 4,000 MRI scans each year and conducted more than 8,500 mammograms in the previous year. The donation adds to the couple’s previous support for the Kauaʻi hospital, where their earlier gifts have funded medical equipment, telemedicine, COVID-19 relief and emergency-care improvements.The $1.48 million gift is intended to keep MRI services available while Wilcox Medical Center renovates its existing MRI suite. The hospital said the renovation is expected to take at least eight months, creating a need for an alternative location for patients who require MRI examinations during the construction period.The mobile MRI unit will allow Wilcox to continue offering the service without interrupting access while the permanent imaging space is being upgraded.The hospital performs more than 4,000 MRI scans annually, making continued access particularly important for patients who rely on the facility for diagnostic imaging.The donation comes as Wilcox expands its imaging capabilities on Kauaʻi. The hospital's broader imaging programme includes MRI, mammography, X-ray, ultrasound, nuclear medicine and interventional radiology services.A portion of the donation will also fund a new 3D mammography machine and the renovations required to install it at Wilcox Medical Center.The hospital conducted more than 8,500 mammograms in the previous year, according to Wilcox officials. Wilcox was also the first medical centre on Kauaʻi to offer 3D mammography, beginning in 2010.The hospital has highlighted the importance of advanced breast-imaging technology for women in Hawaii, where dense breast tissue can make cancer detection more difficult. Wilcox's Women's Center currently provides mammography, breast imaging, biopsies and other specialised women's health services.The new equipment will add to Wilcox's existing diagnostic capabilities and help the medical centre continue providing breast-imaging services on the island.The $1.48 million donation is part of a longer history of support from Chan and Zuckerberg for Wilcox Medical Center.According to the hospital, the couple have contributed more than $4 million to Wilcox through five separate donations supporting equipment, programmes and services. Their earlier contributions included funding for telemedicine initiatives, COVID-19 relief efforts and renovations to the hospital's emergency department and trauma centre.Their previous major imaging donation came in 2022, when Chan and Zuckerberg gave $1.8 million to help Wilcox reach its $4 million fundraising goal for an upgrade to one of its CT scanners. The new CT system replaced a model installed in 1999 and was designed to provide faster, higher-quality imaging while using a lower radiation dose.That earlier contribution was separate from the new $1.48 million donation for MRI and mammography services.Wilcox Medical Center is a not-for-profit hospital in Līhuʻe that has served Kauaʻi since 1938. It is part of Hawaiʻi Pacific Health and is the largest medical centre on the island, offering a broad range of specialties and programmes.The hospital's location makes access to specialised medical technology particularly significant for island residents. Wilcox describes its role as providing healthcare close to home, while its imaging services allow patients to receive diagnostic scans without routinely having to travel elsewhere for care.The hospital is also Kauaʻi's only Level III Trauma Center and a Primary Stroke Center, adding to its role as a major healthcare provider for the island community.The Wilcox donation forms part of Chan and Zuckerberg's broader philanthropic involvement in Hawaii. The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative says Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg have committed more than $100 million to more than 100 Hawaii nonprofit organisations since 2016.Their Hawaii philanthropy has included support for healthcare, education, conservation, community development and other local initiatives. The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative also supports the Kauaʻi Medical Training Track at the University of Hawaii's John A. Burns School of Medicine.The initiative's community website also lists the Wilcox donation among its Hawaii community work, describing the May 2026 contribution as support for new imaging technology at the medical centre.
Article Summary: Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg have donated $1.48 million to Wilcox Medical Center in Līhuʻe, Hawaii. The donation will fund a mobile MRI unit and a new 3D mammography machine, as well as renovations needed to install the equipment. The mobile MRI will allow the hospital to continue providing scans while its existing MRI suite undergoes an expected eight-month renovation.

Article Title: White House bars CNN from Air Force One press pool for Trump's upcoming trip
Article Text:
Earlier last week, Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House.

The White House has replaced CNN with conservative network Real America’s Voice (RAV) in the television press pool covering President Donald Trump’s trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, on Saturday.According to White House guidance, RAV was listed as the secondary television correspondent and crew for the out-of-town travel pool, while CNN was not named as the primary television pool member.Trump is scheduled to attend a college football game between the University of Tennessee and the University of Texas at midday Saturday.The move came shortly after CNN journalists, along with reporters from MS NOW and Politico, returned to the White House with television cameras after a judge granted the three news organisations a temporary reprieve from the administration’s restrictions on their access.Earlier last week, Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House. The move also prevented the outlet from flying aboard Air Force One and carrying out its scheduled pool duties when Trump travelled to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.A judge later blocked the administration from enforcing the ban on the three outlets and ordered it to restore the credentials of affected reporters.However, the status of the White House press pool remained less clear.With CNN excluded from the television pool, Fox, NBC, ABC and CBS had refused to perform their pool duties until regular access was restored. Coverage resumed on Friday, with CNN serving as part of the pool as Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the National Archives.It remained unclear how the White House’s latest move would affect the ongoing litigation involving CNN, MS NOW and Politico.An outside lawyer representing CNN had previously told CNN anchor Jake Tapper that he believed the restoration of the outlets’ access also covered the White House press pool. MS NOW and Politico are part of separate pool rotations from the five major television networks.A judge has given the news organisations until Monday to file a request for a preliminary injunction, which could keep Trump’s proposed ban on the outlets on hold for a longer period.The television press pool is a key way for audiences around the world to receive video of the president’s speeches and public appearances. It allows one group of journalists to cover events where space is limited and share the footage and information with other news organisations.The White House press pool also includes print, radio and still photography rotations. The system exists partly because presidents frequently travel and speak at locations that cannot accommodate the entire press corps. The Trump White House also produces its own content, including livestreams of presidential events.
Article Summary: Real America’s Voice (RAV) will cover President Donald Trump's trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, on Saturday. Earlier last week, Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House. The move also prevented the outlet from flying aboard Air Force One and carrying out its scheduled pool duties.

Article Title: Shailene Woodley joined scientists in the Sargasso Sea to collect microplastics; why this remote Atlantic ecosystem became a real-world pollution laboratory
Article Text:
PC: TIME/National Geographic

The Sargasso Sea became the focus of a scientific expedition

PC: National Geographic

The plastic pollution hidden beneath apparently clean water

One Sargasso Sea sample contained 1,298 microplastic fragments

A remote ecosystem is also a nursery for marine life

The Sargasso Sea expedition became part of a bigger campaign

The pollution story reaches far beyond the Sargasso Sea

A laboratory without walls

Woodley's ocean work continued after the expedition

Why the Sargasso Sea matters to microplastic research

Far from the beaches and busy coastlines where plastic pollution is easiest to see, scientists found evidence of a much less visible problem in the Sargasso Sea. During a 2019 Greenpeace expedition, actress Shailene Woodley joined researchers collecting samples from the remote North Atlantic ecosystem, where floating Sargassum provides habitat for marine life. As reported by Greenpeace, one sample contained 1,298 microplastic fragments, highlighting how tiny pieces of plastic can accumulate even in distant ocean waters. The findings placed the Sargasso Sea within a wider debate about marine pollution, while Woodley's involvement connected the scientific expedition with a campaign for stronger protection of international waters.Woodley joined Greenpeace on an expedition to the Sargasso Sea in 2019, travelling with scientists who were collecting samples for microplastic research. The location mattered because the Sargasso Sea is a remote open-ocean ecosystem rather than a heavily developed coastal environment.The Sargasso Sea is an area of the North Atlantic defined by ocean currents rather than a physical shoreline. Those currents help concentrate floating material in particular parts of the ocean. Plastic that has broken down into progressively smaller pieces can remain in the water column and move with these circulation patterns, allowing researchers to examine pollution far from the places where much of the original material was used and discarded.That made the expedition useful for a broader question. If plastic fragments could be detected in such an isolated marine environment, the problem could not be understood simply as a matter of litter washing up on a beach.The material being collected was not the sort of plastic waste that can be picked up by hand. Microplastics are generally tiny fragments or particles produced when larger plastic items break apart, although some are manufactured at small sizes. Their scale changes the way pollution behaves in the sea. Larger objects can sometimes be tracked, removed or photographed. Much smaller fragments can become dispersed through seawater and interact with marine organisms in ways that are considerably harder to see.The Sargasso Sea therefore offered researchers a place to examine a form of pollution that can be present without creating an obvious visual sign. A stretch of blue water can appear clean while containing thousands of minute plastic particles.That contrast is part of what made the expedition scientifically useful. The absence of visible rubbish did not necessarily mean the absence of plastic.During the Greenpeace expedition, scientists recorded high concentrations of microplastic in the North Atlantic. One sample contained 1,298 microplastic fragments, a figure reported as exceeding levels found in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.The comparison is striking because the Sargasso Sea is not normally associated with the enormous accumulation of floating debris that has made the Pacific region famous. Yet the sampling showed that significant concentrations of tiny plastic particles could exist in another remote ocean system.A single sample cannot describe every part of the Atlantic, and concentrations can vary considerably depending on currents, location, depth and sampling conditions. What the expedition provided was a snapshot of pollution within an ecosystem that is otherwise difficult to observe from land.The Sargasso Sea has another reason for attracting scientific attention. Its floating mats of Sargassum provide habitat in the open ocean, where shelter can be limited.The ecosystem is associated with juvenile sea turtles and other marine organisms that use the floating vegetation as habitat and feeding grounds. The relationship between plastic pollution and these organisms is therefore an important part of the wider research question.Microplastics do not remain neatly separated from marine ecosystems. Small particles can be encountered by organisms at different levels of the food web. Understanding exactly what happens after exposure is complex and depends on the species, the type of plastic, the concentration and other environmental conditions.For scientists working in the Sargasso Sea, the issue is consequently larger than measuring plastic alone. The samples provide evidence about what is present in the water within a living ocean environment.Woodley's involvement brought a recognisable public figure into a scientific campaign, but she had concerns about celebrity environmentalism before agreeing to take part.She wanted to know what Greenpeace intended to do with the expedition and how the information gathered at sea would feed into wider action. Her position, as described by National Geographic, was that taking part only made sense if the work extended beyond a photograph or a social media post.That approach became part of her longer involvement with Greenpeace's campaign for stronger protection of international waters. The Sargasso Sea expedition was connected to the organisation's work around the High Seas Treaty, an agreement intended to create a legal framework for conserving marine areas outside national jurisdiction.Woodley later took part in advocacy aimed at policymakers and United Nations officials, rather than treating the expedition as a standalone environmental appearance.The significance of the expedition lies partly in what it says about the geography of plastic pollution. Plastic entering the ocean does not necessarily remain close to the source. Currents can transport floating material over considerable distances, while sunlight, waves and physical abrasion can gradually break larger objects into smaller fragments.That creates a difficult research problem. By the time a scientist finds a microplastic particle in an offshore sample, its original source may be impossible to identify. The Sargasso Sea offers an unusually clear example of this problem. It is geographically remote, yet it is connected to the wider Atlantic circulation system. The plastic found there is part of a much larger movement of material through the ocean.Calling the Sargasso Sea a pollution laboratory does not mean it is an artificial testing site. It is the opposite. The value comes from studying pollution under real ocean conditions, within an ecosystem shaped by currents, floating vegetation and marine life.Scientists can collect water samples, count particles and identify the types of plastic present. Those measurements can then be considered alongside information about the area's currents and biology.The work also illustrates why microplastic research often begins with something as simple as a water sample. Much of the problem cannot be understood from photographs of beaches or large pieces of floating rubbish. The smaller material requires sampling and laboratory analysis. In the Sargasso Sea, the ocean itself becomes the study environment.The 2019 expedition was one part of a wider period of environmental campaigning for Woodley. Her involvement with ocean issues later included public advocacy for the High Seas Treaty and appearances connected with marine conservation.As reported by Sustainable Fisheries UW, she also appeared in the 2024 PBS documentary series Hope in the Water, in an episode examining overfishing and alternatives to conventional seafood. The programme looked at ways seafood production and consumption could place different pressures on marine ecosystems.Her environmental work has not been limited to the ocean. Before turning more heavily towards marine conservation, Woodley became involved in grassroots organising around the Dakota Access Pipeline protests in 2016. She had also worked on voter canvassing in rural California, experiences that introduced her to organisers working outside the entertainment industry.The Sargasso Sea expedition sits within that longer pattern. The setting was remote, the pollution was largely invisible, and the scientific work depended on gathering evidence rather than simply documenting what could be seen from shore.The expedition offered a useful reminder that marine plastic pollution is not confined to crowded coastlines or recognisable garbage patches. Tiny fragments can occur in remote parts of the Atlantic, including waters that support distinctive ecosystems.For scientists, the Sargasso Sea provides a place to examine that problem within the ocean itself. The samples collected there help reveal what is present beneath an apparently clean surface, while the surrounding biology raises questions about how persistent plastic particles interact with marine life. That is what turned the remote Atlantic region into a pollution laboratory. The sea did not need to be covered in visible rubbish for researchers to find evidence of human waste. The particles were already dispersed through the water, small enough to be missed by the naked eye but measurable when scientists went looking for them.
Article Summary: The Sargasso Sea is an area of the North Atlantic defined by ocean currents rather than a physical shoreline. One sample contained 1,298 microplastic fragments, exceeding levels found in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. Microplastics are generally tiny fragments or particles produced when larger plastic items break apart. Their scale changes the way pollution behaves in the sea.

Article Title: A Chicago couple began protecting their Illinois woodland in the 1980s rather than develop it; decades later, all 126 acres have been bought for a new public preserve carrying their family name
Article Text:
Representative image from Canva

A different decision in the 1980s

Planting thousands of trees

The ancient bur oak

A preserve along Horse Creek

From private land to public preserve

The family name will remain

Why private conservation matters

A living woodland, not just open space

Planning the public future

A conservation legacy that took decades

In the 1980s, Dr. Shin Theke Kang and his wife, Tae Sue Kang, made a long-term decision to protect a piece of land in southwestern Will County, Illinois, rather than develop it. Over the decades, the Chicago couple restored former agricultural areas, planted thousands of trees and cared for the woodland along Horse Creek. Now, all 126 acres have been acquired by the Forest Preserve District of Will County and will become Horse Creek Preserve, Kang Woodland. The announcement, reported by WJOL, marks the transition of a privately protected landscape into a public natural area. The property contains more than 32,000 surviving trees, including black walnut, oak, maple, ash, pine and cherry, as well as a historic bur oak believed to be hundreds of years old. The new preserve will carry the family name as a lasting tribute to their conservation efforts.When Dr. Shin Theke Kang and Tae Sue Kang acquired the Illinois property, they could have viewed it as land for future development or agricultural use. Instead, they chose to preserve it.The couple began protecting the property in the 1980s, when much of the surrounding landscape was still shaped by farming and other human activity.Their decision was not a short-term project. It became a decades-long effort to care for the land and improve its natural character.Some portions of the property had previously been used for agriculture. The Kangs began reforesting those areas so they could complement the older trees that had remained along Horse Creek.That approach required patience. Newly planted trees need years to become established, and not every sapling survives. The couple continued the work even though the full ecological benefits would not be visible immediately.Today, the result is a mature landscape that contains woodland, open areas and a creek corridor. What began as a private conservation decision has now become the foundation of a public forest preserve.The Kangs hired a company to plant approximately 40,000 trees across the property. Many survived without irrigation, according to the Forest Preserve District and local reports.The surviving trees include black walnut, oak, maple, ash, pine and cherry. Together, they form a varied woodland rather than a single-species plantation.A diverse tree community can provide different types of habitat throughout the year. Some trees produce nuts or fruit, while others offer nesting spaces, shade and shelter. A mixture of species can also make the woodland more resilient to disease, pests and changing weather conditions.The planted trees now stand alongside legacy trees that were already growing near Horse Creek. That combination gives the property both young and mature habitat.Reforestation also changes the physical character of the land. Tree roots help stabilise soil, fallen leaves return nutrients to the ground and branches create cover for birds, mammals and insects.The Kangs’ work therefore involved more than adding trees to an open field. It helped rebuild a functioning woodland ecosystem over many decades.One of the property’s most notable natural features is a large bur oak that is thought to be hundreds of years old.The tree had been growing along Horse Creek before the Kangs began their restoration work. It represents a link to the landscape that existed before much of the surrounding land was cleared or cultivated.Bur oaks are particularly important in the Midwest. Their thick branches, rugged bark and large acorns provide shelter and food for wildlife. Older trees can also contain cavities and deadwood that support birds, bats, insects and other organisms.A tree that has survived for centuries can serve as a living record of the region’s environmental history. It has endured changes in land use, storms, droughts and generations of human activity.The newly planted trees may eventually reach a similar age, but the bur oak gives the preserve an immediate sense of deep time. It is one of the natural landmarks that makes the property more than a recently created woodland.The new preserve is located in Custer Township in the southwestern part of Will County. The property follows Horse Creek, which flows into the Kankakee River near the Wauponsee Trail.Creek corridors are valuable because they connect different parts of a landscape. Waterways provide drinking and breeding areas, support vegetation and offer routes for wildlife to move between habitats.Trees along streams can shade the water, reduce erosion and help maintain cooler conditions for aquatic organisms. Fallen leaves and branches also contribute organic material to the creek and surrounding soil.The connection to the Kankakee River places the property within a wider watershed. Actions on the land can influence water quality downstream, making forest protection important beyond the boundaries of the preserve itself.The creek also adds a distinctive feature for future visitors. People may experience the preserve not only as a woodland but as a landscape shaped by flowing water, changing seasons and the relationship between forest and stream.On September 9, 2026, the Forest Preserve District of Will County purchased the 126 acres. The property will be known as Horse Creek Preserve, Kang Woodland.The acquisition means that the land will no longer depend solely on private ownership for its protection. The district will manage it as part of the county’s public forest preserve system.That transition can create new opportunities for residents. Public preserves may offer trails, nature observation, educational programs, volunteer activities and other forms of access, depending on the property’s development and management plans.The preserve will not necessarily be opened all at once. Staff may need to assess the land, identify sensitive habitats, plan access routes and determine how to protect the creek and mature trees.A careful opening process can help balance public enjoyment with ecological protection. Natural areas can be damaged by unmanaged foot traffic, invasive species, litter and disturbance during breeding seasons.The district’s responsibility will be to make the woodland available while preserving the conditions that make it valuable.Naming the preserve Kang Woodland creates a permanent connection between the family and the property.Many conservation stories focus on public agencies or large organisations, but the early work here was carried out by two private landowners. The Kangs protected the property long before it became part of the county preserve system.Their name will remind visitors that the woodland exists because someone made a decision decades earlier to preserve and restore it.The name also recognises the difference that individual landowners can make. A single property may appear small compared with a county or regional landscape, but it can provide a vital piece of habitat and create a link between other protected areas.By carrying the Kang name, the preserve will tell its history as people walk through the trees. The land will be public, but its conservation legacy will remain personal.A large amount of wildlife habitat exists on privately owned land. Owners decide whether to develop, farm, restore or protect their property.Private conservation can fill gaps in public land networks. A property may contain a wetland, forest or creek corridor that connects two larger natural areas. Protecting it can help animals move through the landscape and reduce habitat fragmentation.The Kangs’ project also demonstrates the value of long-term ownership. Because they maintained the property over several decades, they were able to see the effects of restoration and preserve features that might otherwise have been lost.Their decision did not rely on an immediate financial return. The benefits developed gradually through tree growth, habitat formation and improved ecological connections.When the public acquisition finally occurred, the Forest Preserve District received more than undeveloped acreage. It acquired a landscape that had already been cared for and shaped by conservation.The 126 acres will provide more than scenic views.The forest can support songbirds, woodpeckers, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and insects. Different tree ages create different nesting and shelter opportunities, while fallen logs and leaf litter provide habitat near the ground.The creek and its edges may support aquatic organisms, waterfowl and animals that depend on wet environments. Open areas can provide space for wildflowers and pollinators.A healthy woodland also contributes to broader environmental functions. Trees absorb carbon dioxide, release oxygen, reduce erosion and help slow stormwater. Their roots improve soil structure, while their canopies moderate temperatures.These benefits become more valuable as surrounding land is developed. A protected woodland can serve as a refuge for species that lose habitat elsewhere.The preserve may also provide educational value. Students, families and local residents can observe seasonal changes, learn about native trees and see how restoration develops over time.The Forest Preserve District purchased the property under its 2025 to 2030 capital improvement program, which includes funding for new land acquisitions. A local report said the district paid approximately $1.3 million for the property.The purchase is the first step in creating the public preserve. Future work may include surveys, trail planning, signage, habitat management and the removal of invasive plants.Any public access plan will need to account for the property’s ecological sensitivity. Horse Creek, mature trees and newly established woodland all require protection.Staff may also monitor how visitors use the property after it opens. If certain areas become heavily disturbed, the district could adjust routes or limit access during particular seasons.The goal is to make the preserve welcoming without treating it like an ordinary park. Its primary purpose is to protect natural resources, while recreation and education can be designed around that mission.The story of Kang Woodland is a reminder that environmental restoration rarely happens quickly.The Kangs began protecting the property in the 1980s. They planted tens of thousands of trees, restored former agricultural land and preserved older woodland along Horse Creek. Decades later, the land has become a 126-acre public preserve.The timeline matters. A tree planted in the 1980s is now large enough to contribute meaningfully to the forest. A decision that once affected only one family’s property now benefits an entire community.The preserve also shows how private action and public conservation can work together. The Kangs protected and restored the land, while the Forest Preserve District secured its future and created the possibility of public access.Horse Creek Preserve, Kang Woodland, will stand as both a natural area and a record of long-term stewardship. Its trees carry the evidence of years of care, and its name will honour the couple who chose preservation when development might have seemed easier.What began as a private woodland in Illinois has now become a public inheritance for future generations.
Article Summary: Dr. Shin Theke Kang and his wife, Tae Sue Kang, made a long-term decision to protect a piece of land in southwestern Will County, Illinois, rather than develop it. Over the decades, the Chicago couple restored former agricultural areas, planted thousands of trees and cared for the woodland along Horse Creek. Now, all 126 acres have been acquired by the Forest Preserve District of Will County and will become Horse Creek Preserve, Kang Woodland.

Article Title: ‘Long skirts, good mothers': Italian minister sparks outrage over sexist remarks
Article Text:
Italian minister apologises after remarks linking skirt length to marriage

Italy’s foreign minister Antonio Tajani has faced backlash after suggesting that women who wear longer skirts are more suitable for marriage and more likely to make good mothers.“My children are married,” he said. “But if I had to advise a young man which woman to marry, I would suggest a less flashy but more reliable, more serious woman, who will certainly be a good mother.“Ready to provide the necessary answers, always present. Perhaps less pretty, with a slightly longer skirt. But while with the attractive one you might get a few ‘cornettos’, with the other you are certainly sure of everlasting love. She will keep her promise to marry and ensure the stability of the home. She will be there," he added.Over the past week, several female MPs and senators have condemned Tajani’s remarks, wearing mini-skirts and shorter skirts in protest after the Italian foreign minister commented on what kind of woman a man should marry.The 73-year-old deputy prime minister later apologised for the remarks, which he made during a political event on Friday.His comments sparked strong criticism from politicians across Italy, with former prime minister and current Florence Senator Matteo Renzi calling them “backwards”.Renzi also shared an AI-generated image of Tajani wearing a short denim mini-skirt in a satirical response to his remarks.Addressing the controversy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week, Tajani said he had been “misunderstood” and apologised for any offence his remarks may have caused, according to comments reported by Italian media.“I apologise if people felt offended by what I said, but I never intended to offend women, and I never have, either in my private or my public life,” he said.The controversy comes as Italy prepares to ban the burqa and niqab in schools, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announcing on Sunday that her government would soon take the measure to the Cabinet.Meloni also proposed limiting the number of foreign students in each classroom and requiring parents of foreign students facing serious integration difficulties to learn Italian. The government has not yet specified the proposed limit on foreign students.
Article Summary: Antonio Tajani said women who wear longer skirts are more suitable for marriage and more likely to make good mothers. The 73-year-old deputy prime minister later apologised for the remarks, which he made during a political event on Friday. Several female MPs and senators have condemned Tajani’s remarks, wearing mini-skirts and shorter skirts in protest.

Article Title: Iran offers US 7-day plan to end war, reopen Strait of Hormuz
Article Text:
The Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a central bargaining point in efforts to end the conflict

Tehran seeks phased route out of war

Iran has offered the United States a seven-day plan to end the nearly seven-month war in West Asia, with Tehran proposing that the Strait of Hormuz be reopened by the end of the seventh day if certain conditions are met, The New York Times reported.Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strategic waterway and the US and Iran would restart comprehensive negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear programme. Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said the proposal had been conveyed to Washington through intermediaries and was similar to a memorandum of understanding reached by the two sides in June.“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators that if certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be open on the end of the seventh day and talks would restart...it would be better, if a deal was reached before the U.S. midterm elections,” Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations General Assembly, according to the report.The proposal comes as both sides remain publicly committed to diplomacy but sharply divided over the terms of any settlement. US President Donald Trump has threatened to “annihilate” Iran if no agreement is reached, while also indicating that a deal could be possible.The Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a central bargaining point in efforts to end the conflict. Reuters, citing Iranian, regional and Western diplomatic sources, reported that negotiators in New York were exploring a phased arrangement under which Iran would reopen the waterway in return for the US lifting its economic blockade.A senior Iranian official said a possible arrangement could begin with an end to the US blockade and the reopening of Hormuz, followed potentially by access to frozen Iranian assets. The sources said the main difficulty was that neither side wanted to surrender its leverage first.The negotiations also face the challenge of ensuring that any agreement is durable enough to prevent a repeat of an earlier understanding that collapsed in July. Trump has said he believes a deal could potentially be reached after the November 3 US midterm elections.A White House official, however, said Trump remained open to talks only “under the right circumstances”, while arguing that Washington was in a strong negotiating position because of the pressure on Iran's economy and the situation around Hormuz.
Article Summary: Iran has offered the United States a seven-day plan to end the nearly seven- month war in West Asia. Tehran proposes that the Strait of Hormuz be reopened by the end of the seventh day if certain conditions are met. Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strategic waterway and the US and Iran would restart comprehensive negotiations.

Article Title: 19-year-old lost his lamp in an Australian cave in 1953, survived three days, became a NASA scientist; 68 years later, students found the lamp still hanging
Article Text:
Professor Brian O’Brien and the carbide lamp he lost inside an Australian cave in 1953. Image: ABC

A short cave trip turned into a 75-hour survival ordeal

The lost lamp remained in the cave for decades

Britanny Meers who recovered the lamp

Two students spotted the lamp 68 years after it was lost

Volunteer cavers spent two hours reaching it in 2026

The teenager became a NASA scientist and the lamp will now be displayed

Brian O’Brien was 19 when he entered the Yarrangobilly Caves in New South Wales in December 1953 with fellow caver Fred Stewart, but a short exploration turned into a three-day fight for survival. The pair became separated inside East Deep Cave, and O’Brien eventually lost the carbide lamp that was his only source of light after slipping and falling. He spent about 74 to 75 hours underground with little food and only a small amount of water before rescuers found him. O’Brien later became a NASA scientist and worked on lunar dust experiments carried aboard Apollo missions. His abandoned lamp remained inside the cave for decades. In 2021, two students discovered it about 60 metres underground, still hanging from a rocky ledge, before a volunteer caving team recovered it in 2026. This remarkable story demonstrates how a single terrifying ordeal underground ultimately connected across decades to a young man's extraordinary journey toward becoming a pioneering space scientist.O’Brien and Stewart were members of the Sydney University Speleological Society and had travelled to Yarrangobilly after finishing their university examinations.On December 15, 1953, they explored West Deep Creek Cave before deciding to have a quick look inside East Deep Creek Cave on their way back to camp. As their carbide lamps began running low, they started making their way towards the entrance, but O’Brien stayed behind to investigate another section. He became disoriented and was left alone in an unfamiliar part of the cave. His lamp eventually failed, leaving him in darkness. During his attempt to find a way out, he hooked the lamp onto a rock wall, then slipped and fell and could no longer locate it. The search became a major rescue operation, with more than 50 people eventually involved in efforts to locate the missing student. O’Brien was eventually found alive after rescuers followed his calls and reached him deep inside the cave. He eventually heard rescuers after about 75 hours underground.O’Brien survived his ordeal, but the lamp stayed behind in the cave. For decades, it became a small but memorable part of his story, particularly because he continued to want it recovered. O’Brien's daughter, Ros O’Brien, told ABC that her father never stopped looking for the lamp and always wanted to bring it back. Brian O’Brien died in 2020 at the age of 86, meaning he did not live to see the object found. The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service later said the lamp remained undiscovered for more than 70 years, while the exact location of the object was eventually identified by a new generation of cavers.The lamp was finally spotted in 2021 by Brittany Meers and her friend Lachlan Bailey, who were students and exploring the cave as cavers. They found the relic roughly 60 metres underground, where it was hanging from a high ledge. At the time, they did not immediately understand its historical significance and left it in place. The discovery later became known within the caving community, prompting discussions about how it could be safely recovered while respecting the cave environment and the O’Brien family's wishes. The finding came 68 years after O’Brien had lost the lamp during his 1953 ordeal, creating the second chapter of a story that had begun more than six decades earlier.Four volunteer cavers, including Meers, returned to the cave in 2026 to retrieve the lamp under a recovery mission coordinated with NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service. The route was difficult, with the team squeezing through narrow spaces and scrambling across challenging sections in temperatures that could fall to about 5 degrees Celsius. Although the lamp was only about 100 to 150 metres into the cave in a straight line, the obstacles made the journey considerably more difficult. After about two hours underground, the group reached the lamp and successfully removed it from the rock where it had remained since 1953. The object was reportedly in remarkably good condition, with surprisingly little corrosion after more than seven decades underground.The recovered lamp became an unexpected link between two very different parts of O’Brien's life. After surviving his cave ordeal, he went on to become a prominent space scientist specialising in lunar dust. An Australian government citation records that O’Brien served as a NASA principal investigator, invented the Apollo Dust Detector Experiment and developed experiments that were deployed on Apollo missions including Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15. His family has entrusted the recovered lamp to NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, which plans to preserve and display it at Yarrangobilly. Ros O’Brien and her son Bobby Cafagna travelled from Perth to witness the recovery, with the family describing the moment as a fitting end to a story that began when a 19-year-old became lost in the darkness.
Article Summary: Brian O’Brien was 19 when he entered the Yarrangobilly Caves in New South Wales in December 1953. A short exploration turned into a three-day fight for survival. The pair became separated inside East Deep Cave, and O'Brien eventually lost the carbide lamp that was his only source of light after slipping and falling. He spent about 74 to 75 hours underground with little food and only a small amount of water before rescuers found him. His abandoned lamp remained inside the cave for decades. In 2021, two students discovered it about 60 metres underground, still hanging from a rocky ledge

Article Title: In 1888, George Vanderbilt began building a vast North Carolina estate; 26 years later, his widow sold 86,700 acres for $433,500, helping create the core of Pisgah National Forest in 1916
Article Text:
Building a cradle of forestry

Anchoring public land conservation

Enduring environmental heritage

A major property deal that began more than a century ago with a grieving widow turned a huge private wilderness in North Carolina into one of the most important public conservation achievements in American history. In May 1914, Edith Vanderbilt agreed to sell 86,700 acres of valuable mountain forest from the private Biltmore Estate to the United States federal government for $433,500. The deal was made at $5.00 per acre and moved the huge forest area into public ownership. The land later became the foundation of Pisgah National Forest, which was formally established in 1916. The sale carried out the conservation plan of her late husband, George Washington Vanderbilt. He began buying worn-out farmland and mountain slopes near Asheville, North Carolina, in 1888. Over 26 years, he collected more than 125,000 acres to build a self-sufficient mountain retreat centered around the 250-room Biltmore House.When George Vanderbilt first bought land in Western North Carolina, years of uncontrolled logging and burning had badly damaged local watersheds and forests. To restore the land, Vanderbilt hired famous landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted and young forestry expert Gifford Pinchot, who later became the first chief of the United States Forest Service.Under their direction, the Biltmore property became a testing ground for scientific forest management and soil restoration across the American South. In 1898, German forester Carl A. Schenck founded the Biltmore Forest School on the estate. It became the first school of professional forestry in North America. After George Vanderbilt unexpectedly died in March 1914 from complications following surgery, keeping the huge private property became a major financial burden for his widow. Edith Vanderbilt chose to follow her husband's wish to preserve the mountain wilderness instead of selling the land to commercial timber companies. According to historical records documented by the Forest History Society, Edith wrote directly to United States Secretary of Agriculture David F. Houston on 1 May 1914 to formally offer the land to the federal government. In her letter, she explained that she wanted the land protected for the public. She wrote: "I wish to sell this tract of land to the Government at a price significantly below its commercial value in order that my husband's plan for the protection of these mountain forests may be permanently realized."The purchase was made possible by the Weeks Act, a federal law passed by the US Congress in 1911. It allowed the federal government to buy private land in eastern states to protect the headwaters of navigable rivers and manage forest resources. The National Forest Reservation Commission, led by Secretary Houston, soon approved the deal. Official commission records in the Forest History Society archives show that the government viewed the $5-per-acre price as an exceptional bargain. Private timber companies had offered much more for the right to harvest the forests. The transaction was completed in 1914, leaving only 10,000 acres around the main Biltmore House and its immediate grounds in private family ownership. On October 17, 1916, President Woodrow Wilson issued an executive proclamation creating Pisgah National Forest, with the former Vanderbilt land forming its central area.The purchase protected important headwater areas for major river systems in the region, including the French Broad River basin. Today, Pisgah National Forest covers more than 500,000 acres across the Appalachian Mountains. Millions of people visit the forest each year for hiking, scientific research, and wildlife conservation. The birthplace of American forestry is still preserved within the forest at the Cradle of Forestry in America National Historic Site. The site stands on the same grounds where Schenck's students once attended their original field lectures. By accepting a much lower price for the land, Edith Vanderbilt protected both the financial future of the remaining estate and a large area of North American wilderness for future generations. The deal remains one of the largest single land purchases made under the Weeks Act and helped set an example for protecting public land across the eastern United States.
Article Summary: In May 1914, Edith Vanderbilt agreed to sell 86,700 acres of valuable mountain forest to the United States federal government for $433,500. The deal was made at $5.00 per acre and moved the huge forest area into public ownership. The land later became the foundation of Pisgah National Forest, which was formally established in 1916.

Article Title: Kentucky man won $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in 2025; now arrested for fifth time after being found intoxicated in Walmart car park
Article Text:
Police found Kentucky Powerball winner asleep in a running Mustang

How James Farthing won Kentucky's record Powerball prize

Florida arrest came shortly after the jackpot win

February arrest involved an intimidation charge

Burglary and marijuana charges followed in March

July domestic violence case involved strangulation allegations

Fifth arrest adds to Farthing's legal cases

James Farthing, a Kentucky man who won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025, has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol-related impairment. The incident adds to a series of legal cases involving Farthing since his jackpot win. He had shared the historic prize with his mother, Linda Grizzle, after purchasing a $2 ticket from a Georgetown retailer.Earlier incidents included an April 2025 arrest in Florida, where Farthing was accused of kicking a sheriff’s deputy during an altercation. He later pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery and obstruction or resisting arrest. In February 2026, he faced an intimidation charge, followed by burglary and marijuana-possession charges in March after being accused of entering a Lexington home and stealing $12,000. In July, he was arrested on domestic violence-related charges, including first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault. Farthing has pleaded not guilty to the domestic violence charges.This troubling pattern illustrates how sudden wealth can sometimes exacerbate existing personal struggles rather than resolve them, highlighting the complex psychological challenges lottery winners frequently face.The latest incident began shortly before 3 a.m. on Sunday, September 20, when a caller reported a white Ford Mustang stopped in the middle of an intersection in Georgetown, Kentucky. The vehicle later moved to a Walmart car park on Osborne Way, according to the arrest citation reported by WKYT.Deputies arrived and found the Mustang parked near an electric vehicle charging station with its engine running. Farthing was reportedly asleep in the passenger seat. Officers knocked on the window several times before he woke up.The arrest citation described several signs of impairment, including the smell of alcohol and marijuana, bloodshot and watery eyes, slurred speech and difficulty maintaining balance. Farthing was subsequently charged with being intoxicated in a public place and taken to the Scott County Detention Center.According to the arrest report, Farthing told deputies that a woman had driven him to the car park and left him there. Authorities reviewed surveillance footage, which reportedly showed no one exiting the Mustang after it entered the car park.Farthing purchased the winning Powerball ticket from Clark's Pump N Shop in Georgetown. The ticket matched the required numbers in the April 26, 2025 drawing, resulting in a $167.3 million jackpot.The Kentucky Lottery identified the prize as the largest Powerball jackpot ever won in the state. Farthing and his mother, Linda Grizzle, claimed the winnings together and announced that they would share the fortune.The pair chose the lump-sum option, with the cash value of the jackpot reported at about $77.3 million before taxes. The winning ticket itself cost just $2 and was purchased at Clark's Pump N Shop in Georgetown.The win brought significant attention to the family, while Farthing later appeared in news reports concerning several encounters with law enforcement in Kentucky and Florida.Farthing's first reported arrest after winning the lottery took place in Florida in April 2025. Authorities accused him of battery involving a law enforcement officer and resisting arrest following an incident at a hotel.According to the Associated Press, officers said Farthing kicked a deputy in the face during an altercation and attempted to flee. He faced charges connected to the confrontation.The Independent later reported that Farthing pleaded guilty in the case and received a sentence of time served and $1,000 in fines.In February 2026, Farthing was arrested in Georgetown on a charge involving intimidation of a participant in a legal process. The case followed a report from a woman who contacted emergency services and said she feared for her safety.According to People, police investigated an incident at Farthing's home and reportedly found a woman hiding under a desk. Authorities also searched the property and allegedly discovered a handgun, ammunition, marijuana and drug paraphernalia.Farthing faced additional charges in March 2026 in connection with allegations of burglary and marijuana possession. Authorities accused him of entering a Lexington home and stealing approximately $12,000 in cash.The Guardian reported that investigators used security camera footage during the investigation. Farthing was later reportedly located at a casino.Local news reports said the burglary and marijuana charges were dismissed in May. The dismissal applied to those specific charges and did not resolve his other legal cases.In late July 2026, Farthing was charged with first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault following a reported domestic violence incident in Scott County.Police said a woman reported that a verbal argument became physical after a boating trip. According to the arrest report, she alleged that Farthing placed both hands around her neck and restricted her breathing. Authorities also reported visible marks on her neck.Farthing pleaded not guilty through his legal representative. A judge set his bond at $15,000 and ordered him to avoid contact with the alleged victim. He was also required to wear an electronic monitoring device with a notification feature.The September arrest is the fifth reported arrest involving Farthing since he won the Kentucky Powerball jackpot in 2025.The latest case concerns public intoxication in Scott County and follows the July domestic violence-related arrest. His legal proceedings remain separate from the lottery win, which he shared with his mother.As of September 23, 2026, the public intoxication case remained pending in Scott County District Court, with no confirmed outcome of the scheduled arraignment.The jackpot that promised a new beginning has instead been followed by a string of legal troubles. Fortune's wheel turns without warning, and wealth offers no guarantee of a steady life.
Article Summary: James Farthing won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025. He has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol- related impairment.

Article Title: Meet Lidia Rak, the 18-year-old Florida student whose research found a correlation between groundwater radium and pediatric brain-tumor incidence; her school says her advocacy contributed to a $30 mil
Article Text:
Meet Lidia Rak, the 18-year-old Florida student whose research found a correlation between groundwater radium and pediatric brain-tumor incidence (Image Credit: Duval County Public Schools)

How Rak's research began

From student research to cancer advocacy

What the $30 million bill means in her story

What comes next for the 18-year-old

At 18, Lidia Rak has already taken her interest in cancer research beyond the classroom and into conversations with lawmakers. The Mandarin High School senior began looking at cancer data after a personal experience with an autoimmune blood condition led her to learn more about cancer risks. Her research eventually turned towards pediatric brain tumours and the possible relationship between naturally occurring radium in groundwater and reported cases in Florida. Rak then began advocating for greater attention to childhood cancer research and care. According to her school, Mandarin High School, that work also contributed to a $30 million Florida bill supporting local hospitals.Rak told Duval County Public Schools that her research started with leukemia and cancer data. She had been interested in blood conditions because of her own childhood diagnosis of an autoimmune blood condition, which she said increased her risk of developing cancer. While looking at cancer cases in Florida, her focus eventually shifted to brain tumours. The turning point came when she was reading research about possible cancer clusters in the Jacksonville area. The earlier work had examined whether airborne carcinogens could help explain the clusters but had not found a statistically significant connection. Rak noticed that the researchers had not examined possible waterborne carcinogens. That gap prompted her to ask a different question: could something in the water be associated with the pattern of pediatric cancer cases?She began examining available data and looking specifically at radium levels in groundwater alongside pediatric brain-tumour incidence.According to Rak's account to her school, her analysis identified a correlation between the two. The distinction between correlation and causation is important here. Rak's research identified a statistical relationship in the data she examined; that finding by itself does not establish that groundwater radium causes pediatric brain tumours. Her school describes the work as an environmental epidemiology study.Rak did not stop with the research. She began using what she had found to talk about pediatric cancer funding and support. As a National Gold Together Ambassador for the American Cancer Society, she has spoken with lawmakers in Florida and Washington, DC. She told Mandarin High School that her conversations with legislators were not simply about presenting statistical figures. Instead, she tried to explain the presence of cancer clusters in the Jacksonville area and why she believed more attention should be given to pediatric cancer research and patient support.Her interest in childhood cancer is also tied to what she sees as a gap between pediatric and adult cancer care. According to Rak, she became more aware of differences in funding while working as a national ambassador for the American Cancer Society. The Barron Prize for Young Heroes also recognised this combination of research and advocacy when it named Rak among its 2026 winners. The prize described her work as an independent environmental epidemiology study examining the relationship between naturally occurring radium in drinking water and pediatric brain-tumour incidence in Florida. It also said she had used the research to advocate for increased pediatric cancer research funding.Rak's advocacy has also taken her into state policy discussions. Mandarin High School reported in April that she had contributed to a $30 million Florida bill supporting local hospitals. The school described this as one of the outcomes of her work as a student researcher and advocate. For Rak, the policy work grew out of a broader concern about how pediatric cancer is researched and treated. She told her school that childhood cancer may receive less funding than adult cancers despite the long-term effects that a diagnosis can have on children.Her advocacy has therefore gone beyond her original research question. The groundwater-radium project gave her one way to examine a potential environmental factor, while her work with the American Cancer Society gave her an opportunity to discuss pediatric cancer funding more broadly.Rak is planning to continue both her scientific and advocacy work. She told Mandarin High School that she intends to study molecular biology in college and eventually pursue medicine, with the goal of becoming a pediatric oncologist. She also plans to remain involved with the American Cancer Society and continue working on brain-tumour research. She is also working on a book about youth advocacy. Rak said the project is aimed at young people who want to get involved but may not know where to begin. She has spoken about her own experience of finding a starting point through a volunteer opportunity and gradually becoming involved in cancer advocacy.Her story has now earned recognition beyond her school and state. The Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes selected Rak as one of its 2026 winners, part of a group of 25 young people recognised for projects involving service, science, health and the environment.For Rak, the research and advocacy appear to be connected by the same goal: understanding issues that affect children and finding ways to draw greater attention to them. Her groundwater research offers a specific statistical association to investigate further, while her advocacy has given her a platform to push for more discussion and funding around pediatric cancer.
Article Summary: Lidia Rak, 18, found a correlation between groundwater radium and pediatric brain-tumor incidence in Florida. She then began advocating for greater attention to childhood cancer research and care. Her work contributed to a $30 million Florida bill supporting local hospitals. The Barron Prize for Young Heroes recognised this combination of research and advocacy.

Article Title: $30bn tariff cut, Iran and AI dialogue: Key points from Xi-Trump talks
Article Text:
Xi-Trump talks: Tariff cuts, Iran, AI dialogue and more shape US-China ties

$30 billion

tariff reduction

framework

Focus on drugs and energy

Global issues and strategic stability

Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up his three-day state visit to Washington on Friday, announcing that he will meet US President Donald Trump twice more before the end of the year, taking the total number of face-to-face meetings between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies in 2026 to four.The visit focused on strengthening the US-China relationship, with the two sides reaching agreements and setting up mechanisms covering trade, investment, energy, drug trafficking, critical minerals and emerging technologies. Trump and Xi also discussed global issues including the war in Iran, while agreeing to maintain dialogue and pursue a relationship based on strategic stability, respect, fairness and reciprocity.The visit was criticised by some in the US as heavy on ceremony but light on substantive breakthroughs, with no major progress announced on issues including trade or the safety of artificial intelligence. The two leaders, however, sought to project continuity in their efforts to preserve a stable relationship and agreed to continue discussions on several areas in the months ahead.The state visit, which concluded on September 25, marked the first visit by a Chinese president to the White House in more than a decade.The two countries operationalised the US-China Board of Trade and the US-China Board of Investment, which were established after the May 2026 summit in Beijing.Under the Board of Trade, the two sides reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. The board also launched a working group on market access barriers in agriculture.US exports covered under the recommendations include agricultural goods, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices, while US imports include consumer products such as small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children’s car seats.China will also import at least 10 million metric tons of US coal in 2027 and again in 2028.The Board of Investment will provide a government-to-government channel to discuss investment opportunities and investment-related barriers. Separately, the two countries agreed to continue work on US concerns over supply shortages involving rare earths and other critical minerals, with the aim of restoring shipments to appropriate levels.China and the US had already been working on a reciprocal tariff reduction framework covering $30 billion worth of products from each side.The United States welcomed China’s scheduling of orphines, a class of deadly drugs, and noted China’s new export controls on two fentanyl precursor chemicals. Washington also encouraged the permanent scheduling of these and other substances and chemicals to curb the flow of illicit precursors to drug producers in North America.The United States said that, acting on information from US law enforcement, China arrested 21 Chinese citizens in August 2026 for the manufacture and distribution of precursor chemicals to illicit drug producers in North America. The US also encouraged maximum sentences, including the death penalty where applicable.Trump also urged Xi to increase the production of refined petroleum products to help stabilise global supply.New dialogue on ‘super intelligence’The two leaders agreed to use the term “super intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence” for applicable emerging technologies.The US and China established the U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue to exchange views on the risks and benefits linked to such technologies, with the next exchange scheduled for November 2026. They also agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel for incidents involving super intelligence.The two countries also agreed on a $30 billion reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement and to launch dialogue on AI under an eight-point consensus reached during Xi’s visit, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.Trump and Xi discussed Russia, North Korea and Iran and agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. They also agreed that no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways.The two leaders agreed to support each other as the respective hosts of the G20 and APEC, with both intending to attend each other’s summits.Trump also advocated trilateral arms control negotiations involving the United States, Russia and China.The leaders recalled that the United States and China had been allies during World War II and fought together in the war. Trump also highlighted the US forward military presence in the Indo-Pacific, which the White House said had contributed to generations of American prosperity.
Article Summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up his three-day state visit to Washington on Friday. He will meet US President Donald Trump twice more before the end of the year. The visit focused on strengthening the US-China relationship. The two sides reached agreements and set up mechanisms covering trade, investment, energy and drug trafficking.

Article Title: In 2011, Philadelphia began a $2 billion plan to turn hard blocks into rain gardens and porous streets; by 2021 it kept an estimated 3.08 billion gallons of stormwater out of waterways each year
Article Text:
A planted rain garden with grasses, stone beds and drainage inlets illustrates green stormwater infrastructure designed to capture, slow and infiltrate runoff before it reaches the sewer system. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A city built above underground streams

A twenty-five-year bet on

green infrastructure

A landscaped stormwater swale uses grasses, gravel and shallow drainage channels to collect and filter rainwater, demonstrating how green infrastructure can manage runoff before it enters conventional drains. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A model that other cities are eyeing on

Philadelphia is one of the oldest cities in America, and for decades its water-absorbing streets, rooftops, and sidewalks were progressively covered with hard surfaces, until the pipe networks beneath them could no longer handle the runoff. The city struggled with this for many years before taking an environmentally focused approach to resolving a grave infrastructural issue.Some 60 percent of Philadelphia uses what engineers call a combined sewer system, in which rainwater and domestic sewage flow together through the same pipes to treatment plants. That system works in dry weather, but heavy rain can overwhelm the pipes, sending a mix of stormwater and untreated sewage into rivers and streams. For a community between the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, this meant billions of gallons of filthy water finding its way into local waterways every single year.By the early 2000s, the problem was too big to ignore, and Philadelphia officials began searching for an alternative to the standard solution of creating huge underground storage caverns and tunnels, an approach estimated to cost the city as much as nine billion dollars. Eventually, the Environmental Protection Agency approved a totally different strategy, one centred on softening the city rather than merely burying more concrete beneath it.In 2011, Philadelphia began Green City, Clean Waters, a twenty-five-year programme with an investment of approximately $2.4 billion. It was structured on rain gardens, tree trenches, porous pavement and vegetated planters that were designed to soak up stormwater before it ever reaches a sewer line. Rain was no longer seen as waste to be drained away as quickly as possible but as a resource to be captured, slowed down and allowed to seep organically into the ground. Streets that had poured every drop of rain directly into the sewer system were repaved with materials that allowed water to seep through, and empty lots and schoolyards were recontoured into little basins that could catch storm runoff.Since the initiative began, the Philadelphia Water Department has supervised the roll-out of more than a thousand of these green stormwater projects city-wide, spread throughout parks, sidewalks, transit corridors and private properties.
