A decade into the plan, by 2021, the Philadelphia Water Department reported that this network of small-scale interventions was keeping an estimated 3.08 billion gallons of polluted stormwater out of the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers every year, a volume that would otherwise have poured straight into the city's waterways during heavy rain.The individual components of this system are intentionally tiny and unglamorous, and that is part of why the total achievement is easy to miss. One rain garden may only collect a small amount of water from one block, one porous parking lot may soak up runoff from one storm and one row of street trees may slow rain on its way down. But multiplied across thousands of such sites across the city, the cumulative impact is that a significant portion of Philadelphia’s overall stormwater burden is being handled before it ever gets to an outdated pipe network.Philadelphia's approach has gained attention far beyond its borders, and NACTO has profiled it as one of the largest green street projects at city scale, noting that the programme has deployed green infrastructure across more than 28,000 acres of the city's combined sewer area. Part of the attraction is the economics. It has generally been cheaper to build green infrastructure over thousands of smaller sites than to build a few enormous subterranean tunnels and it has ancillary benefits no concrete tunnel ever could, from shaded streets and reduced summer heat to slightly higher property prices in the communities where the work has been done.And none of this indicates the initiative has outright solved Philadelphia's stormwater problem. Rainfall patterns have intensified since the plan was first drawn up in 2009, and the city may eventually need to combine its green strategy with more grey infrastructure to keep up with larger storms. But even so, the core assumption underlying Green City, Clean Waters, that a city can make a real reduction in sewage pollution by rethinking its streets, not just its pipes, has already changed how planners in other flood-prone areas think about stormwater.Delegations from other cities often visit Philadelphia to learn how the programme was conceived, financed and implemented on this scale, and numerous towns have subsequently drafted their versions of green stormwater plans, taking Philadelphia’s approach as the starting template. Whatever the city ultimately does to adapt to the increased rainfall, the core premise that redesigning streets and vacant lots can compensate for the massive subsurface infrastructure has shown that street redesign can help reduce pressure on subsurface infrastructure, one rain garden and permeable pavement at a time.
Article Summary: Philadelphia is one of the oldest cities in America. For decades its streets, rooftops, and sidewalks were progressively covered with hard surfaces, until the pipe networks beneath them could no longer handle the runoff. In 2011, the city began Green City, Clean Waters, a twenty-five-year programme with an investment of approximately $2.4 billion. It was structured on rain gardens, tree trenches, porous pavement and vegetated planters.

Article Title: In 1985, a 10-year-old threw a message bottle into the Atlantic; 37 years later, a Florida family found it and mailed his childhood note back to him
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a 10-year-old boy releasing a handwritten message in a glass bottle into the Atlantic off Florida in 1985. Credits - Google Gemini

A childhood note sealed in glass

The storm brings the past ashore

An AI-generated representative image shows a weathered message bottle that was discovered on a Florida beach decades after its release into the Atlantic. Credits - Google Gemini

Today’s floating bottles and the quiet science

For generations, kids on beach vacations have tried the same straightforward experiment. Half expecting the sea to take their words to some far stranger, they scribble a little letter, fold it inside a bottle, and hurl it into the waves. Most of these bottles are lost at sea, buried in sand, or broken against rocks. Occasionally, however, a child's note reappears decades later and reaches someone who has long forgotten who wrote it. That's precisely what happened to a Kentucky man whose message drifted in the Atlantic for 37 years before a family on the Florida coast found it and traced it back to him.It was 1985, and ten-year-old Troy Heller was on a family holiday in Vero Beach on the Atlantic coast of Florida. He wanted to attempt something he had never done before. He scribbled a brief letter, asking whoever found it to call or write him, included his contact details, put the paper in an old glass Pepsi bottle and tossed it into the sea. It was the kind of modest, hopeful gesture most children make and then forget about. Heller was no exception. He grew up and resided in Mount Washington, Ky, and never gave the bottle another thought.Way before satellites, government scientists used this precise kind of sealed bottle to investigate how water travelled over the oceans, a procedure with a remarkably deep institutional history. Agencies in the United States have cast thousands of drift bottles into the sea since the eighteenth century, requesting finders to report the date and site of discovery so researchers may chart ocean circulation, as the NOAA Ocean Service has detailed in its archives. Some of those scientific bottles floated back up after decades at sea, a chronology not far different from what Heller’s personal note would eventually undergo.The bottle’s reappearance coincided with one of the more odd weather phenomena of 2022. That November, Hurricane Nicole hit the coast near Vero Beach, another uncommon late season storm, and only the third hurricane on record to strike the US mainland in November, after the 1935 Yankee Hurricane and 1985's Hurricane Kate . Beaches all along Florida's eastern coast, including parts badly ravaged weeks earlier by Hurricane Ian, churned up in the storm and dislodged all manner of long-buried debris.Heller's bottle was among the objects that came ashore, recovered on a beach near Sebastian, Florida, about 13 miles north of where it was first tossed. The Carrmax family discovered it while helping to remove storm debris. They opened the bottle and found a legible note with a phone number attached, then set out on a quest to track down its author. Their investigation took them right to Heller in Kentucky, who was shocked to be shown evidence of something he had done as a boy and never expected to hear about again.Most message bottles are never recovered at all, lost to the sea long before anyone finds them. It counts as a statistical rarity, not a common occurrence: a glass bottle that survives nearly four decades of tides, storms and salt water, only to be found by people determined to track down a stranger a thousand miles away.Heller’s account is somewhere between folklore and a very real branch of oceanography that’s still going on now, just with far more powerful instruments. Researchers no longer use glass vials for this kind of work. Instead, they use satellite-monitored buoys that work on the same basic idea but automatically communicate their position, delivering real-time information to weather and climate models. Today, NOAA’s Global Drifter Program has more than a thousand of these buoys drifting around the world’s oceans at any given moment, and the data they produce helps forecasters understand everything from surface currents to the behaviour of storms like Nicole.His bottle was never going to be a scientific instrument but a child's secret hope that someone, somewhere, would read his words. But it travelled the same secret routes that buoys and research vessels take every day, showing in the most personal way imaginable exactly how far and how long the ocean can carry something little. Nearly forty years later that same interest came back to him, brought home by a hurricane and a family of strangers who thought to look a little harder at what the storm had left behind.
Article Summary: Troy Heller, 10, wrote a note in a glass bottle and tossed it into the Atlantic in 1985. The bottle was found on a beach near Sebastian, Florida, 37 years later. The Carrmax family discovered it while helping to remove storm debris. They opened the bottle and found a legible note with a phone number attached, then set out on a quest to track down its author.

Article Title: 'October 7 attack equal to sixteen 9/11s': Israeli PM Netanyahu in UN speech
Article Text:
He also defended Israel's military action against Iran

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack was, in proportionate terms, equivalent to 16 September 11 attacks in the United States.Recalling the attack, Netanyahu said Hamas militants had killed about 1,200 people in Israel, including civilians, and abducted 251 others.“These Hamas monsters, they slaughtered Holocaust survivors. They burned babies alive in front of their parents. They beheaded our men. They brutally raped our women. And then they murdered them. Altogether, they slaughtered 1,200 Israelis that day. I want to give you an idea of what this means for a country of 10 million. Proportionately, this is equal to 40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours. That's 16 times 9/11. 16 9/11s that occurred not very far from here. On that darkest of days, our enemies expected us to collapse. Well, we didn't collapse. Instead, we rose and fought like lions.”Netanyahu's remarks came after days of speeches from world leaders condemning Israel’s war in Gaza and accusing his government of genocide against Palestinians. He rejected the allegations, calling Israeli genocide claims “the biggest lie of the century”.His appearance was marked by a mass walkout, with scores of delegates leaving the chamber as he approached the rostrum. Netanyahu responded by calling those who left “moral cowards”.“In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall,” Netanyahu said. “In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran’s nukes.”He also defended Israel’s decision to attack Iran, saying it was “one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make”, and thanked US President Donald Trump for his actions against Tehran.Netanyahu's speech also addressed violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, which he described as involving a “handful of young juvenile delinquents”. He said, “I can’t stand that. I won’t stand for vigilantism,” while accusing foreign leaders and international media of exaggerating the scale of the violence.His address came as Israel faced growing international criticism over its conduct of the Gaza war. According to the Gaza Health Ministry, at least 73,922 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s subsequent offensive, while Israel maintains control over large parts of the territory and continues military operations.
Article Summary: Netanyahu said the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack was, in proportionate terms, equivalent to 16 September 11 attacks in the United States. He also defended Israel's military action against Iran, saying it was “one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make”

Article Title: In 1981, Chuck Leavell and his wife inherited Georgia land; decades later, Charlane grown into a 4,000-acre estate with 70% forest cover
Article Text:
PC: US Fish and Wildlife Service

How Rose Lane’s inherited Georgia land grew into the 4,000-acre Charlane estate

How Leavell turned a life in rock music into a study of forestry

PC: WSJ

How Charlane's forests became part of a working timber operation

About 70% of the 4,000 acres is forest

The old Bullard House remains part of the property

Forestry became part of Leavell's public life

For Chuck Leavell, the road to becoming a Georgia tree farmer began with land that came to his wife’s family in 1981. At the time, Leavell was already building the music career that would take him from the Allman Brothers Band to decades of work with the Rolling Stones. The inherited property was farmland, not a ready-made forestry operation. Much of the surrounding land had long been used for crops and livestock. Leavell and his wife, Rose Lane, gradually acquired neighbouring tracts and began changing the way the property was managed. As per the reports by Wall Street Journal, what started with roughly 1,000 acres eventually became Charlane Woodlands and Preserve, a 4,000-acre property outside Macon, with about 70% of the land remaining forested.Rose Lane inherited the original acreage after her grandmother died in 1981. The property included family land and a house, making its future a matter of stewardship as much as ownership. Rather than leaving the acreage as it was, the couple began buying adjoining parcels over the years.That expansion changed the scale of the operation. By later accounts, Charlane had reached around 4,000 acres, a substantial increase from the land Rose Lane inherited.The property is now associated with forestry, wildlife habitat and the management of Southern pine, rather than the row crops that had previously dominated parts of the land.Leavell did not arrive at forestry with formal training. He had a different profession entirely.Leavell was already an established keyboard player by the time he took on greater responsibility for the family property. His work with the Allman Brothers Band had placed him in the American rock scene during the 1970s. The connection between his two lives gradually became clearer to him. The instrument at the centre of his career was made from wood, while the land around his home was filled with trees that could be grown, harvested and used. He began reading about land management and forestry, speaking with other landowners and learning about the practical side of running a tree farm.At one point, he studied forestry by correspondence while he was on tour. The education covered areas including forest management, prescribed burning and the longer-term decisions involved in growing timber.The couple's move towards forestry made practical sense for a property that Leavell had to manage alongside a demanding touring career. Crops and livestock require regular attention, while timber operates on a much longer cycle. Charlane's forests include Southern yellow pines such as loblolly and longleaf, along with other native hardwoods. Earlier descriptions of the property also recorded slash and shortleaf pine among the trees being managed.The intention was not simply to leave the woodland untouched. Timber production became part of the property's management, with thinning and harvesting carried out as part of the forest cycle. Leavell has described the process in practical terms, including the satisfaction of knowing that trees grown on his land could eventually become lumber for someone's home.The scale of Charlane is perhaps easiest to understand through the acreage. The property grew to roughly four times the size of the land originally inherited by Rose Lane, reaching about 4,000 acres. Recent profiles put around 70% of Charlane under forest cover. That amounts to roughly 2,800 acres of woodland, although the exact acreage of forest can change with planting, harvesting and other land-management decisions.The forests are not the only feature of the property. Charlane has also been managed for wildlife, with habitat work aimed at species including bobwhite quail, deer, turkey and ducks. Prescribed burning has formed part of the approach, helping manage vegetation and maintain habitat conditions in areas intended for wildlife.There is also a much older layer to Charlane. The Bullard House, an early 19th-century farmhouse, was restored by the Leavells in the 1990s. The property developed beyond a private residence. A guest lodge was built from timber associated with the land, while other buildings have served practical purposes including workshops and accommodation. In a 2014 account, the main house was described as a roughly 6,000-square-foot home with extensive use of Southern yellow pine, from floors to walls and exposed structural elements.A separate woodworking shop became another way for fallen or harvested trees to remain connected to the property. In the earlier account, Leavell described having large sections of an old red oak milled into thick slices that could later be turned into furniture.The work at Charlane eventually extended well beyond the boundaries of the property. Leavell became involved in forestry education and conservation, writing books about forests and appearing in projects focused on trees and land management. His forestry work has also brought recognition. He was named National Outstanding Tree Farmer of the Year in 1999 and has twice been recognised as Georgia Tree Farmer of the Year. The U.S. Forest Service also made him an honorary forest ranger.That record helps explain why Charlane is more than an unusual second career for a touring musician. The property became the place where Leavell could put the forestry principles he was learning into practice, while continuing the musical career that helped make the expansion of the land possible.
Article Summary: Chuck Leavell and his wife, Rose Lane, bought a Georgia property in 1981. The property, Charlane Woodlands and Preserve, is now a working timber operation. About 70% of the 4,000 acres is forested, with habitat work aimed at wildlife.

Article Title: Pakistan govt puts Islamabad on lockdown as Imran Khan’s party pushes ahead with march
Article Text:
Islamabad locked down as PTI prepares for Imran Khan march

Leaders of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party have vowed to press ahead with nationwide demonstrations demanding his release, as authorities tightened security in Islamabad ahead of the planned march.More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads, while sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed across the city.The government has also deployed security personnel in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and closed the main highway linking the provincial capital, Peshawar, with Islamabad. The sweeping security measures have fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with several businesses struggling to receive supplies.The measures to prevent Khan’s PTI from proceeding with the march come amid mounting concerns over the treatment of the former prime minister, who has been in jail since August 2023 following convictions in multiple cases.On Friday, PTI leaders announced that they would postpone the start of the march to October 4, a week after the original September 27 date, saying they hoped the delay would put further pressure on the government.The planned protest also comes amid the detention of three of Imran Khan’s sisters. Aleema Khan was detained last week, followed by Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, who were ordered to remain in custody for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance.
Article Summary: More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads. Sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed.

Article Title: Pakistan goes bananas over giant gorillas dancing to Bollywood songs
Article Text:
Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online (Photo: AFP)

Pakistanis are going bananas over a trend that has crossed the Indian border: Giant gorillas, dancing to Bollywood music.Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online, turning them into the surprise stars of weddings, birthdays and other festivities.In the videos, guests can be seen joining in alongside the costumed entertainers, many of them visibly delighted by the unusual addition to their celebrations. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding DJ tracks while partygoers gather round and dance, creating a lively, comic spectacle that has quickly drawn attention across social media.Behind the trend in Lahore is Shayen Zahoor, who runs Gorilla.co.pk, a business offering giant dancing gorilla acts for events across the city.Speaking to AFP, Zahoor explained how quickly the idea took off. He said the costume was ordered in early April and arrived by the end of the same month, after which the team wasted no time putting it to use.Once the suit arrived, he and his team lost no time getting started."We uploaded a reel on Instagram, and within just two days it reached a million views," Zahoor recalled.The overwhelming response convinced them to treat the venture as a serious business, and bookings soon began pouring in, with the public reaction proving remarkably enthusiastic."On the very first day, we received approximately 1,200 to 1,300 messages," he said, describing how curious would-be customers flooded his inbox.Many wanted to know whether the costume had genuinely arrived, what it would cost to book, and other practical details before making up their minds.What began as a single Instagram reel has since snowballed into a full-fledged entertainment phenomenon, with giant gorillas now a familiar, if unlikely, fixture at Pakistani celebrations.
Article Summary: Giant dancing gorillas have become a popular feature at Pakistani celebrations. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding DJ tracks while partygoers gather round. A single Instagram reel has since snowballed into a full-fledged entertainment phenomenon. The trend has even crossed the Indian border.

Article Title: Pakistan govt crackdown forces PTI retreat? Imran's party likely to postpone Sept 27 Islamabad march
Article Text:
Imran Khan has been in jail since 2023

Pakistan minister says PTI has 'run away'

(With PTI inputs)

The Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) has decided to postpone its planned march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4, party insiders said on Friday.The PTI had planned the march to the capital to demand the release of its incarcerated founder and former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan . The decision to delay the protest apparently came in response to the tough measures taken by the federal government to prevent it.According to PTI sources, the decision was taken at a party meeting and will be formally announced by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister and PTI leader Sohail Afridi.Earlier in the day, Afridi had asserted at a press conference in Peshawar that the planned long march would go ahead despite road blockades and other measures. However, he expressed concern over reports of nails being driven into roads at the provincial boundaries, questioning whether a conspiracy to “cut” Khyber Pakhtunkhwa off from the rest of Pakistan had formally begun.“Our long march will definitely take place. This time, we will definitely come out. Put nails on the roads, place containers or fire bullets, we will come out. We will end this corrupt system of fake rulers,” he told reporters.“Pakistan will not break at any cost and we will save Pakistan,” he added.Cricketer-turned-politician Khan, 73, has been held at Rawalpindi’s high-security Adiala Jail since 2023, when he was arrested following his conviction in a corruption case.Pakistan information minister Ataullah Tarar reacted to the reports by saying the PTI had “run away” because it had made “no preparations” for the march to Islamabad.“There are no preparations for the PTI’s long march either, and that is why they have backed out of this protest. If they have the courage, let them come and hold the march,” Tarar said.The federal government had placed shipping containers along Islamabad’s main roads, allowing them to be closed at short notice ahead of the planned march.Hotels in the Faizabad area of Rawalpindi had been closed, while restaurants and shopkeepers were directed to shut their businesses. Guest houses and transport terminals in Faizabad had also been ordered to close from Friday night.Thousands of security personnel were deployed in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, the capital’s twin city and home to Pakistan Army headquarters, to control Khan’s supporters.Tensions over the planned protest continued despite PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan urging the government to open negotiations and warning against confronting political workers with force.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) has decided to postpone its planned march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4. The PTI had planned the march to the capital to demand the release of its founder and former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan. Khan has been held at Rawalpindi’s high-security Adiala Jail since 2023, when he was arrested following his conviction in a corruption case.

Pak PM skips questions at UN

Hafiz Saeed named in terror cases

India hits out at Pakistan at UN

Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday declined to answer questions from reporters about Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) founder Hafiz Saeed during his visit to the United Nations headquarters for the 81st UN General Assembly.As Sharif entered the UN headquarters, reporters asked him, “Prime Minister, when will you stop harbouring terrorists?” Sharif did not respond. Later, as he left the premises, he was again asked when Pakistan would prosecute Saeed, but the prime minister once again declined to answer.Hafiz Muhammad Saeed, founder of the proscribed LeT, is a designated terrorist under India's Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and is wanted as an accused in the 26/11 Mumbai terror attack case.The National Investigation Agency has also named Saeed as an accused in its supplementary chargesheet in the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack case.
